title: Thinking and memory: how your brain learns and remembers

summary.text: You can hear ten words once and lose most of them by the next day. Turn the same ten words into a silly story, and most of them stay. Your brain is made of billions of nerve cells called neurons, and every memory is held in the links between them. What you do with something while you learn it decides how strong those links become. Practice makes the links stronger, so a hard skill slowly becomes easy. Even grown-up brains keep changing this way: London taxi drivers grow a bigger part of the brain that finds the way.
summary.art: A child at a dining table telling a story with her hands, while above her head a few glowing dots are joined by lines, some thin and some thick.

intro.hook: What did you eat for breakfast yesterday? What did you eat for breakfast on the same day last month? Why is one easy and the other so hard?
intro.text: Your brain kept yesterday's breakfast, but let last month's go. In this unit you find out how your brain holds on to things. You test two ways of learning a list of words, and see which one lasts until tomorrow. You practise something hard with your other hand and watch it get easier. You find out what neurons are, and why practice changes them. And you try the tricks that people with very strong memories use.
intro.art: A plate with two idlis and a little bowl of chutney, and next to it a faded, blurry plate, as if seen through mist.

outcomes: I can say what my brain does: it senses, thinks, remembers and moves my body, using nerve cells called neurons.
I can name three kinds of memory: memories of things that happened, facts I know, and skills I can do.
I can explain that practice makes the links between neurons stronger, so a skill gets easier and a memory lasts longer.
I can test a way of remembering fairly, and say what I think, what I saw, and why.
I can use three ways to remember better: making a story or a picture, putting things into groups, and testing myself on different days.
I can say why some popular ideas about the brain are wrong, such as 'we use only 10% of our brain'.
I can give examples of other living beings who learn and remember, such as bees and the touch-me-not plant.

terms.meaning: The soft organ inside your skull that senses, thinks, remembers, feels and controls your body.
terms.example: When you catch a ball, your brain sees the ball, works out where it will go, and moves your hands.
terms.art: A side view of a child's head with the brain drawn inside the skull, in soft pink.

terms.meaning: A nerve cell. Neurons carry messages as tiny electrical signals. Your brain has about 86 billion of them.
terms.example: When you touch a hot tumbler, neurons carry the message from your fingers to your brain in a fraction of a second.
terms.art: One neuron: a round middle with many short branches on one side and one long thin tail on the other.

terms.meaning: The tiny gap where one neuron passes its message to the next. The message crosses the gap as a chemical.
terms.example: Each neuron has synapses with thousands of other neurons, like one person passing notes to many friends.
terms.art: The tail end of one neuron almost touching a branch of another, with tiny dots crossing the gap.

terms.meaning: Anything you have learned and kept: a thing that happened, a fact, or a skill.
terms.example: Remembering your grandmother's face, knowing that 2 + 2 is 4, and knowing how to ride a cycle are all memories.
terms.art: Three bubbles: a birthday cake, the sum 2 + 2 = 4, and a child riding a cycle.

terms.meaning: The memory that holds a few things for a few seconds, while you use them. It is also called working memory.
terms.example: Holding an OTP number in your head for the few seconds it takes to type it in.
terms.art: A child looking at a phone screen with six digits, then typing them on another phone.

terms.meaning: The memory that keeps things for days, years or a whole life.
terms.example: Your name, your home, the words of a song you know well.
terms.art: A grandmother and a girl looking at an old family photo album together.

terms.meaning: Bringing a memory back into your mind without being shown it.
terms.example: Saying all the planets without looking at a list is recall.
terms.art: A child with eyes closed, counting on her fingers.

terms.meaning: Losing a memory, or losing the way to bring it back. Most forgetting happens in the first day after learning.
terms.example: You learn a new friend's name at a wedding and lose it by the next morning.
terms.art: A name written in chalk on a slate, half rubbed out.

terms.meaning: A curved part deep inside the brain, one on each side, that helps store new memories of events and places. Its name is Greek for 'seahorse', because of its shape.
terms.example: Your hippocampus helped you remember where you kept your slippers last night.
terms.art: A seahorse beside a small curved brain part of the same shape.

terms.meaning: Doing something again and again to get better at it.
terms.example: Playing the same sarali varisai on the veena every day until your fingers know the way.
terms.art: A girl sitting on the floor playing a veena, with a small notebook of practice ticks beside her.

terms.meaning: The brain's way of changing itself as you learn. Links between neurons that are used get stronger, and new links grow. 'Plastic' here means able to change shape, like clay.
terms.example: After a month of practice, your brain's links for skipping rope are stronger, so you skip without thinking.
terms.art: A lump of clay being pressed into a new shape by a child's hands.

terms.meaning: Grouping many small things into a few bigger pieces, so they are easier to hold in memory.
terms.example: A mobile number like 98410 23456 is easier to remember as two groups of five than as ten separate digits.
terms.art: Ten loose beads, and next to them the same beads on two short strings of five.

terms.meaning: The memory of how to do something with your body. You use it without thinking about the steps.
terms.example: Tying your shoelaces or swimming. You can do it, but it is hard to explain each step in words.
terms.art: Two hands tying a shoelace in a bow.

terms.meaning: Something you have done so often that you do it without deciding to.
terms.example: Washing your hands as soon as you come home, without anyone telling you.
terms.art: A child at a wash basin, washing hands, with a school bag dropped by the door.

explanations.context: This card is about the jobs your brain does every second of the day.
explanations.definition: The brain is the organ that senses the world, thinks, remembers, feels and controls the body.
explanations.description: Your brain sits inside your skull, floating in a liquid that protects it. A grown-up's brain weighs about 1.3 kilograms, about as much as a full one-litre bottle of water and a bit more. Messages come in from your eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. Your brain puts them together, works out what they mean, and decides what to do. It sends messages out to your muscles to move you. It also runs things you never notice, like your breathing and your heartbeat. Your brain is only about 2% of your body's weight, but it uses about one fifth of the energy from your food.
examples: When an auto honks behind you, your brain hears it, works out where it is, and makes you step aside, all in under a second.
While you sleep, your brain keeps your heart beating and your lungs breathing.
When you read a word, your brain turns black marks on paper into a meaning.
explanations.art: A child crossing a lane carefully, with dotted lines from her eyes and ears to her head, and from her head down to her legs.

explanations.concept: Neurons: how the brain sends messages
explanations.context: This card is about the cells your brain is made of, and how they pass messages.
explanations.definition: Neurons are nerve cells. They carry messages as tiny electrical signals, and pass them on to other neurons across tiny gaps called synapses.
explanations.description: Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. A neuron has many short branches that receive messages, and usually one long tail that sends them on. A message travels along the neuron as a small electrical signal. At the end, the message must cross a tiny gap, the synapse, to the next neuron. It crosses as a chemical. Each neuron has synapses with thousands of other neurons. So the brain is a huge web of links. Every thought, feeling and memory is many neurons sending signals together.
examples: Neurons also run from your brain down your back and out to your fingers and toes, so a message can go from your toe to your brain.
Brain scientists can record the electrical signals of neurons with small sensors on the head.
The longest neurons in your body run from the bottom of your back to your toes.
explanations.art: A web of neurons, each with a round middle, branches and a tail, joined to each other by tiny glowing gaps.

explanations.context: This card is about how something you see or hear becomes a memory, and why most things are lost.
explanations.definition: A memory is made when a pattern of neurons that fired together becomes linked more strongly, so that the same pattern can fire again later.
explanations.description: First, something must get your attention. Things you do not notice are not stored at all. Then your short-term memory holds it for a few seconds. Most grown-ups can hold about 7 digits this way, and a child of 8 about 5. If you use it, think about it or link it to something you already know, your brain starts to keep it. The hippocampus helps to store new memories of events and places. Over the next days, and especially while you sleep, the memory is linked into the rest of your brain. Memories of skills, like riding a cycle, are kept by other parts of the brain.
examples: You remember the day the power went off at your birthday party, because it surprised you and you talked about it.
You forget what you ate for lunch on an ordinary day last month, because nothing linked it to anything else.
You can still swim after a whole year without swimming, because skill memories last a long time.
explanations.art: Three steps drawn left to right: a child noticing a bright kite, the kite small inside a bubble, then the kite linked by lines to a rooftop and a festival in a bigger bubble.

explanations.context: This card is about why a hard thing gets easier each time you do it.
explanations.definition: When neurons send signals to each other again and again, the synapses between them grow stronger, and new links can grow. This is called brain plasticity.
explanations.description: The first time you do something new, like writing with your other hand, it is slow and wobbly. Your brain is trying many links to find the right way. Each time you practise, the links you use get stronger. The signal passes more easily, so the skill becomes faster and smoother. In 1949 the scientist Donald Hebb suggested that neurons which fire together become more strongly linked. Experiments have since shown this is true. Links you stop using slowly get weaker. That is why a skill you have not practised for a long time feels rusty. Brains keep changing all through life, at any age.
examples: Children who took music lessons for over a year showed changes in the parts of the brain for hearing and finger movement.
London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, grow a larger back part of the hippocampus, which helps find the way.
Practising a little every day works better than practising for a long time on one day.
explanations.art: Two drawings of the same path between two dots: on the left a faint dotted line labelled 'first try', on the right a thick bold line labelled 'after practice'.

explanations.concept: Why we forget, and what helps us remember
explanations.context: This card is about why most new things fade by the next day, and the ways that make memories last.
explanations.definition: We forget most quickly in the first hours and days after learning. A memory lasts longer when we link it to things we know, picture it, group it, and bring it back again on later days.
explanations.description: In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German scientist, tested his own memory for years. He learned lists of made-up syllables, then tested himself later. He found that most of a new list was lost within a day, and after that the forgetting slowed down. Many later studies found the same. What helps? Making a story or a picture from the things to remember. Putting things into groups, called chunking. And testing yourself, which means trying to bring a memory back without looking. Each time you recall it, especially on a new day, the memory gets stronger. Sleep helps too.
examples: A story that links ten words keeps most of them for a day. Repeating the same words over and over keeps far fewer.
Your times tables stay because you said them aloud on many different days.
Trying to say a poem without looking, then checking, works better than reading it again and again.
explanations.art: A line that falls steeply then flattens, drawn as a slide in a park, with a child sliding down it, and a small ladder labelled 'recall again' going back up.

explanations.context: This card is about learning and memory in other living beings, with and without brains.
explanations.definition: Learning means changing what you do because of what happened before. Animals, plants and even single cells learn and remember.
explanations.description: Honeybees learn which flower colours give the most nectar, and remember it for days. A touch-me-not plant folds their leaves when they are touched or dropped. In a 2014 experiment, Monica Gagliano and her team dropped touch-me-not plants a short way again and again, without harming them. After many drops, the plants stopped folding. They had learned that the drop was harmless. They still remembered it almost a month later, without a brain or any neurons. Plants, animals and people all learn, each in their own way. Some scientists call the plant's change a simple automatic response, not real learning.
examples: A dog learns that the sound of a steel plate means dinner is coming.
A crow at your window learns which flat leaves out food.
Slime moulds, which are single-celled, find the shortest way through a maze to their food, and leave a trail that shows where they have already been.
explanations.art: A honeybee on a blue flower, a touch-me-not plant with half their leaves folded, and a girl writing in a notebook, side by side.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: where in you a memory really is.
explanations.description: Scientists agree that memories depend on links between neurons. They have even found, in mice, small groups of neurons that bring back one particular memory when they fire. But a single memory seems to be spread across many parts of the brain, not kept in one spot. And nobody knows how signals between neurons become the experience of remembering your grandmother's face. Here are the main views.
examples: When you remember a festival, the sights, sounds, smells and feelings all come back together, though they are handled by different parts of the brain.
People who lose part of their brain in an accident often keep most of their memories.

perspectives.explanation: A memory is a pattern of strengthened links between neurons, spread across the brain. There is nothing more to it than that.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study memory without brains
perspectives.explanation: Plants, single cells and even cells in a dish keep traces of what happened to them. So memory is older and wider than neurons, and the brain is one way of doing it.
Awareness is the ground of everything, and memory is awareness holding on to what it has met. The brain is the way this happens in a human body.

explanations.art: A girl lying on a mat looking up, with soft lines going from her head out to small pictures of a festival, a grandmother and a kite.

agreed.text: The brain is made of billions of neurons that pass messages to each other across synapses.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have seen neurons and synapses with microscopes since the late 1800s, and recorded their electrical signals.

agreed.text: Practice strengthens links between neurons, and the brain keeps changing all through life.
agreed.evidence: Brain scans of musicians, jugglers and London taxi drivers show changes that grow with practice. Experiments on animals show synapses getting stronger when used.

agreed.text: We forget most quickly in the first day after learning, and recalling a memory on later days makes it last.
agreed.evidence: Hermann Ebbinghaus found this in 1885, and hundreds of later studies with children and grown-ups found the same.

agreed.text: Linking things into a story or a picture, and grouping them, makes them much easier to remember.
agreed.evidence: In 1969 Gordon Bower and Michal Clark found that people who made stories from lists of words remembered far more of them than people who just repeated them.

agreed.text: Sleep helps new memories to settle.
agreed.evidence: People who sleep after learning remember more the next day than people who stay awake for the same time. Recordings from rats show their memory neurons replaying the day's paths while they sleep.

challenging.claim: We use only 10% of our brain.
challenging.who: A very old and popular idea, repeated in films and adverts
challenging.for: Many people feel they could do much more if they tried, so it seems there must be unused brain.
challenging.against: Brain scans show that every part of the brain is active over a day. Damage to almost any part causes a problem. A brain that wasted 90% of itself would not use a fifth of the body's energy.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that most of the brain is never used.

challenging.claim: Your brain stops changing once you are grown up.
challenging.who: Many scientists for much of the 1900s
challenging.for: Children learn new languages and skills much faster than most grown-ups. Grown-ups often find new things hard.
challenging.against: Brain scans show grown-up brains changing as they learn. London taxi drivers grew a bigger part of the hippocampus while they learned the city's streets.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that only children's brains can change.

challenging.claim: Some people are 'visual learners' and some are 'listening learners', and each learns best only in their own way.
challenging.who: Many teachers and books on learning
challenging.for: People do say they like pictures or words more. It feels true that some lessons suit us better.
challenging.against: When scientists tested it, teaching people in their 'own' style did not help them learn more. Most things are best learned with pictures and words and doing, all together.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that each child learns best through one sense.

challenging.claim: Memory works like a video camera, keeping exactly what happened.
challenging.for: Some memories feel very clear and complete, as if we could play them again.
challenging.against: People who remember the same event often remember it differently, and can be sure of things that never happened. Each time we recall a memory, the brain builds it again.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that a memory is an exact recording.

challenging.claim: Only animals with brains can learn and remember.
challenging.for: Learning in people and animals clearly uses neurons, and plants have no neurons.
challenging.against: Touch-me-not plants learned that being dropped was harmless, and kept that memory for weeks. Single-celled beings change what they do because of what happened before.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a brain is needed to learn.

big_questions.q: If your brain changes every time you learn something, are you the same person you were last year?
big_questions.hint: Think about what has stayed the same about you, and what has changed.

big_questions.q: Why did the story list last until the next day, when the repeated list faded?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many links each word had to other things in your mind.

big_questions.q: A touch-me-not plant has no brain, yet learned that being dropped was harmless. So what is a memory made of?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the plant changed, and what your brain changes.

big_questions.q: If you could never forget anything, would that be a good thing?
big_questions.hint: Think about the things you are glad to forget, and what it would be like to remember every lunch you ever ate.

big_questions.q: When you remember your grandmother's voice, where is that voice?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether there is a sound in your head, or something else.

big_questions.q: Is a skill in your hands or in your brain?
big_questions.hint: Think about your other hand, which has the same muscles but not the same practice.

story.title: Paati's Kolam
story.note: The story is made up. The kolam is real: a sikku kolam is drawn as one line that loops round a grid of dots without touching them, and many families in Tamil Nadu draw bigger kolams every morning in the month of Margazhi.
text: It was the first morning of Margazhi, and it was still dark in Madurai. Kavya was eight. She had set an alarm for half past five, because this year Paati had promised to teach her the kolam.

Paati lived with them in a flat on the third floor. Every morning she swept the landing outside their door and sprinkled it with water. Then she bent down with a steel bowl of rice flour and drew. Her fingers let out a thin white line that curled round and round a grid of dots. In two minutes there was a pattern like a flower made of one long loop. The neighbours on the landing always stopped to look.
"This one is a sikku kolam," said Paati. "Seven rows of dots, and one line that goes round all of them. The line never touches a dot, and it ends where it began."
Kavya watched very carefully. She watched Paati's hand go round the first dot, then dip between two dots, then swing round the corner. She was sure she had it.
"Now you try," said Paati. She rubbed out a corner of the landing with her foot and put down fresh dots.

Kavya took a pinch of flour. Her line went round the first dot nicely. Then it went round the second. Then she stopped. Was it under the next dot, or over it? Her line wobbled, crossed itself and ran into a dot. It looked like a tangled thread.
Her little brother Arjun had come out in his banian, rubbing his eyes. "That is not a flower," he said. "That is a noodle."
"I watched you so carefully, Paati," said Kavya. "Why did it all fall out of my head?"

Paati sat down on the step. "Watching is not the same as knowing," she said. "You saw my hand for two minutes. My hand has drawn this kolam every Margazhi for sixty years. Do you think I learned it in one morning?"
"How did you learn it, then?"

"My amma taught me with a little song," said Paati. "Round the top, dip down, round the side, come back. Each part has its words. When you know the words, you do not have to remember seventy turns. You only remember four parts, and then you do them again."
She sang it slowly, and drew one corner of the kolam while she sang. Kavya sang with her. Then Kavya drew the same corner, singing. Her line still wobbled, but it went the right way.
"Good," said Paati. "That is enough for today. Tomorrow you will do it again."
"Only one corner?"
"One corner, every morning," said Paati. "The kolam has to grow a path in your head first. A path grows by walking on it."
So Kavya came out every morning. She made a chart on a sheet of paper and stuck it on the fridge with a magnet. Each morning she timed herself on Amma's phone and wrote down how long the corner took.

On the first day, one corner took her four minutes, and she had to start again twice. On the fourth day, it took two minutes. On the seventh day she drew the whole kolam. It was crooked on one side, but it was one line, and it came back to where it began. Arjun looked at it for a long time. "That is a flower," he admitted.

By the middle of Margazhi, something strange had happened. Kavya could draw the kolam while she talked to the neighbour, Lakshmi Akka, about her school. She did not have to sing the song any more. She did not even have to think. Her hand just knew.
"Paati," she said one morning, "the kolam has moved. It used to be in the song. Now it is in my hand."
Paati laughed. "It is not in your hand, kanna. Your hand is the same hand it was on the first day. Try it with your other hand and see."
Kavya tried with her left hand. The line wobbled and ran into a dot, exactly like on the first morning.
"So where is it?" asked Kavya.

"In your head," said Paati, tapping her own forehead. "Every morning you used the same path, and every morning the path got easier to walk. My old teacher used to say that practice is how you build your own brain. I did not understand her when I was eight. I do now."
On the last day of Margazhi, Arjun came out before anyone else. He was holding the bowl of rice flour.
"Akka," he said, "teach me the song."
So Kavya sat him down on the step, put down seven rows of dots, and showed him the first corner. "Only one corner today," she said. "Tomorrow you will do it again."
story.epiphany: Kavya's hand was the same on the first morning and the last. What had changed was inside her head: every morning of practice had made the path for the kolam a little stronger, until her hand could follow it without her thinking.
ask: Why did Kavya forget the kolam after watching Paati only once?
How did the little song help Kavya remember so many turns?
Why did the kolam go wrong when Kavya tried it with her other hand?
Is there something you can now do without thinking, that was hard when you started?

games.title: I Went to the Santhai
games.context: This is a memory game. A santhai is a weekly market in Tamil Nadu. Each player repeats the whole shopping list and adds one more thing, until someone forgets.

printables.title: 30 market picture cards to cut out
15 memory tokens, 5 for each player
items: Cut out 15 small circles. Each player starts with 5. You lose one each time you forget.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down in a pile. Each player takes 5 tokens.
The first player turns over a card and says: 'I went to the santhai and bought tomatoes.' Then they put the card face down in a row.
The next player turns over a new card, says the whole list in order, and adds the new thing.
If you forget a thing or get the order wrong, lose one token. The next player starts a new list.
After each round, say the trick you used to remember: a story, a picture, or grouping.
When a player has no tokens left, they are out. The last player with tokens wins.
Playing alone: turn over one card at a time and say the whole list each time. How long a list can you say? Try again tomorrow and beat it.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. 2. Shuffle the cards. 3. Give each player 5 tokens.
flow.say: This is a market game. Each of us will say the whole shopping list and add one more thing. If you forget, you lose a token.
flow.kid: Say the whole list. Add one thing. Forget? Lose a token!
flow.context: This is the first step of I Went to the Santhai, a shopping list memory game.

flow.do: Play two rounds. Turn the cards face down as you go, so the list is only in your heads.
flow.say: I went to the santhai and bought tomatoes. Your turn. Say tomatoes, then add your card.
flow.kid: Turn a card. Say the whole list. Add your thing.
flow.parent: Most children manage 6 to 10 things in the first round. Do not help with the list, but after the round, ask which trick they used.

flow.do: After the second round, teach a trick: make a story with the list.
flow.say: Let's try a trick. Make a story as the list grows: the tomatoes rolled into the onions, and a banana slipped on them. Does a story help you go further?
flow.kid: Try making a story as the list grows. Can you go further?

check.q: Divya wants to remember a long market list. Which trick will help her most?
options: Saying each thing very fast
Making a story that joins the things
Shutting her eyes tight
check.why: A story joins each thing to the next, so one brings back the other. Saying things fast does not give them any links. Shutting your eyes can help you picture the story, but on its own it does not join the things.

flow.do: Play one more round with the story trick, then fill in the score sheet.
flow.say: One more round, with stories this time. Then let's write our longest lists on the score sheet.
flow.kid: One more round with a story. Write your longest list.
flow.think: Was the story round longer than the first round? Why?

setup.art: Picture cards of tomatoes, onions and bananas laid face down in a row on a mat, with paper tokens beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Turn a card, say the whole list, add your thing.

setup.art: A girl and her father laughing as she tells a silly story about a rolling tomato.
setup.caption: 2. Try a story to remember a longer list.

games.title: Number Plate Flash
games.context: This is a quick memory game. One player shows a vehicle number plate for five seconds. The other writes it down from memory.

printables.title: 20 number plate cards to cut out

rules: Shuffle the plate cards and put them face down.
The shower turns over one card and shows it for five seconds, then turns it back.
The other player writes the plate from memory.
Score one point for each letter or digit in the right place. A full plate scores 10.
Take turns being the shower. After 5 plates each, add up the scores.
For round two, read each plate in groups before writing: 'TN 59, AB, 12, 34'. Does grouping raise your score?

flow.do: Cut out the cards and explain the game.
flow.say: These are number plates like the ones on cars and autos. The first two letters show the state. TN is Tamil Nadu and KA is Karnataka. I show a plate for five seconds. You write it down.
flow.kid: Look at the plate for five seconds. Then write it down!
flow.context: This is the first step of Number Plate Flash, a memory game with vehicle number plates.

flow.do: Play five plates each and score them.
flow.say: Here is the first one. Look carefully. Five, four, three, two, one. Now write it.
flow.kid: Look hard. Now write it from memory.
flow.parent: Ten letters and digits are more than most people can hold after one look. Most children get 5 to 7 right.

flow.do: Play five more plates each, but this time say each plate in groups before writing.
flow.say: This time, say it in groups as you look: TN 59, AB, 12, 34. Four groups instead of ten letters. Does that help?
flow.kid: Say the plate in groups. Then write it.

check.q: Why does saying 'TN 59, AB, 12, 34' help you remember?
options: You hold four groups instead of ten separate letters and digits
Saying it makes the plate bigger
The letters are easier than the digits
check.why: Your short-term memory can hold only a few things at once. Grouping turns ten small things into four bigger ones. This is called chunking. It is why phone numbers are often written in groups.

flow.do: Compare the two rounds on the score sheet.
flow.say: Which round scored more? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: Which round did better? Why?

setup.caption: 1. Look at the plate for five seconds.

setup.art: The girl writing the plate in a notebook in four groups.
setup.caption: 2. Write it from memory. Next round, group it first.

experiments.title: The Story Trick: does a story help you remember a list?
experiments.context: In this experiment you learn two lists of ten words. You repeat one list, and make the other into a story. Then you see which one you remember, straight away and the next day.
experiments.question: If you make a list of words into a story, do you remember more of them than if you just repeat them?
experiments.predict: You will learn one list by saying each word again and again, and the other by making up a story. Which list will you remember better tomorrow? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both lists have ten words for everyday things in a home. Each word gets the same time, 10 seconds. After each list, you count backwards from 20 to 1, so you cannot keep repeating the words. Only the way of learning changes. You test both lists the next day too, at the same time, without looking.
results_table: My guess: how many I will remember tomorrow
Words remembered the next day (out of 10)

materials.item: the two word lists on this card, read aloud by a grown-up. List A: spoon, pillow, bucket, mango, umbrella, comb, key, tumbler, slipper, clock. List B: broom, candle, banana, towel, coin, bangle, plate, ladder, pencil, kite.
a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook and a pencil for the grown-up to tick the words

schedule.what: Guess first. Learn list A by repeating each word, and list B by making a story. Test both lists straight away.
At the same time of day, without warning and without looking, say all the words you remember from both lists.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two bars for the next day: one for list A and one for list B. Write one sentence about what you found.

flow.do: 1. Read the question aloud. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: I am going to read you two lists of ten words. One you will repeat, and one you will turn into a story. Which list will you remember better tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two lists of words. Repeat one. Make a story with the other. Which will you remember tomorrow? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that list will stay longer?
good: Because saying a word many times puts it in my head.
Because a story is easier to remember than separate words.
Because the story joins the words together.

flow.parent: Do not say what you think will happen. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The guess shows what your child thinks memory is.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Story Trick, where you test two ways of learning a list of words.

flow.do: 1. Read list A aloud, one word every 10 seconds. 2. After each word, your child says it aloud again and again until the next word. 3. Do not show the list.
flow.say: List A. I will say a word. You say it over and over until I say the next one. Ready? Spoon.
flow.kid: Listen to each word. Say it again and again. Keep going until the next word.
flow.parent: List A: spoon, pillow, bucket, mango, umbrella, comb, key, tumbler, slipper, clock. Use the stopwatch to keep 10 seconds for each word. Always do the repeat list first. If you do the story list first, your child may keep making stories with list A too.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to count backwards aloud from 20 to 1. 2. Then ask them to say every word they remember from list A, in any order. 3. Tick each one.
flow.say: Now count backwards from 20 to 1. Then tell me every word you remember from that list. Any order is fine.
flow.kid: Count back from 20 to 1. Then say all the words you remember.
flow.parent: Counting backwards stops your child from repeating the words in their head, so both lists wait the same way. Write the number remembered in the table.

flow.do: 1. Read list B aloud, one word every 10 seconds. 2. After each word, your child adds it to a story, aloud. 3. The story can be as silly as they like.
flow.say: List B is different. This time, make up a story as you go. Each new word must join the story. The first word is broom. What does the broom do?
flow.kid: Make up a story. Every new word must join the story. Silly is good!
flow.parent: List B: broom, candle, banana, towel, coin, bangle, plate, ladder, pencil, kite. A story might go: 'A broom lit a candle and slipped on a banana.' If your child is stuck, ask 'What happens next?' but let them choose the words of the story. Keep to 10 seconds a word, the same as list A.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to count backwards from 20 to 1. 2. Then ask for every word they remember from list B. 3. Tick each one and write the number.
flow.say: Count backwards from 20 to 1 again. Now tell me every word from the story list.
flow.kid: Count back from 20 to 1. Say all the story words.

flow.do: 1. Put the two numbers side by side. 2. Ask what your child notices. 3. Tell them you will ask again tomorrow, but not when.
flow.say: Look at the two numbers. Is there a difference? Tomorrow I will ask you both lists again, without the lists. Which do you think will stay?
flow.kid: Look at your two numbers. Which list did better? What about tomorrow?
flow.parent: Straight away, many children remember 5 to 8 words from each list. The big difference usually shows the next day. Do not let your child practise the lists tonight, or the test will not be fair.

flow.do: 1. The next day, at about the same time, ask for all the words from list A, then list B. 2. Do not give any hints. 3. Write both numbers in the table.
flow.say: Do you remember the two lists from yesterday? Tell me every word you can from the list you repeated. Now every word from the story list.
flow.kid: Remember yesterday's two lists? Say every word you can. First the repeat list. Then the story list.
flow.wait: Do this the next day, at about the same time.
flow.parent: Most children remember far more of the story list the next day, often 7 or more, and only 1 to 4 of the repeat list. If the numbers are close, that is a real result too. Ask your child what they did in their head for each list.

check.q: Meena remembered 3 words from her repeat list and 8 from her story list the next day. What does this show?
options: Story lists always have easier words
Making a story helped her remember more
She is better at remembering on some days
check.why: Both lists had ten words for everyday things, and she tested them on the same day. The only change was the way she learned them. So the story helped. To check the words were not easier, someone else can do it the other way round: list A as a story and list B repeated.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A strong answer: 'I think a story helps me remember. Tomorrow I remembered 8 story words and only 3 repeated words. In the story, each word was joined to the one before, so one word brought back the next.' After your child has answered, read the explanation cards together.

check.q: Why does a story help you remember a list?
options: Each word is joined to others, so one word brings back the next
Stories are louder in your head
Your brain only keeps stories and throws away other words
check.why: In a story, each word is linked to the words around it and to a picture in your mind. When you recall one, it leads you to the next. Repeated words stand alone, so when one is lost, nothing leads back to it. Your brain does keep other words too, but words with more links last longer.

experiments.title: The Other Hand: does practice make it easier?
experiments.context: In this experiment you write the numbers 1 to 10 with the hand you do not usually write with. You time yourself each try, for three days, and see whether practice changes how fast and neat you are.
experiments.question: If you write with your other hand again and again, does it get faster and neater? How fast does it change?
experiments.predict: On the first try, how long will it take you to write 1 to 10 with your other hand? Will your tenth try be faster or slower? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every try uses the same numbers, 1 to 10, in the same boxes, with the same pencil. Time each try with the same stopwatch. Count the numbers that go outside their box. Only the number of tries changes.

materials.item: a printed or hand-drawn sheet with ten rows of ten boxes, each box about 2 cm wide. A four-line English notebook with boxes drawn in pencil works too.
one pencil
a phone stopwatch

experiments.safety: No safety risks. Stop if the hand starts to ache, and rest it.

schedule.what: Write 1 to 10 once with your usual hand. Then four tries with your other hand, timed.
Three more timed tries with your other hand.
Three more timed tries. Make a line graph of your times and talk about what changed.

experiments.record: Fill in the table after every try. On day 3, draw a line graph: tries along the bottom, seconds up the side.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to write 1 to 10 in the first row of boxes with their usual hand, while you time it. 2. Write the time down.
flow.say: First, write 1 to 10 in the boxes with the hand you always use. I will time you.
flow.kid: Write 1 to 10 with your usual hand. Go!
flow.parent: This gives a number to compare with. Most children of 8 take about 10 to 20 seconds.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Other Hand experiment, where you practise writing with your other hand for three days.

flow.do: Ask for a guess about the other hand, and a reason.
flow.say: Now you will use your other hand. How long do you think it will take? Will you get faster if you keep trying? Why?
flow.kid: Now your other hand. How long will it take? Will you get faster? Why?

flow.do: 1. Time four tries with the other hand, one row each. 2. After each try, write the time. 3. Count the numbers that touch or cross the box lines.
flow.say: Off you go with your other hand. Take your time. I will write down the time. Now let's count how many went outside the boxes.
flow.kid: Write 1 to 10 with your other hand. Then count numbers outside the boxes.
flow.parent: The first try is often two or three times slower than the usual hand, and wobbly. Do not let your child switch hands halfway. Praise the effort, not the speed.

flow.do: On day 2, do three more timed tries, the same way.
flow.say: Yesterday you did four tries. Before you start, guess: will today's first try be faster than yesterday's last?
flow.kid: Three more tries today. Is your first try faster than yesterday's last?
flow.parent: Often the first try of a new day is about as good as, or better than, the last try the day before. Sleep helps the brain keep what it practised.

flow.do: 1. On day 3, do three more timed tries. 2. Help your child draw a line graph of all ten times.
flow.say: This is the last day. Three more tries. Then let's draw a graph of all your times, from the first try to the tenth.
flow.kid: Three last tries. Then draw a line of your times.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Look at your graph. What do you think practice did? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Look at your graph. What changed? What shows it? Why?
flow.parent: A strong answer: 'Practice made my other hand faster. My first try took 52 seconds and my tenth took 31. My hand did not change, but the links in my brain for writing with that hand got stronger each time.' Most children's line falls quickly at first, then more slowly.

check.q: Thara's times with her other hand were 60, 51, 46, 43, 42 seconds. What happens to the time she saves on each try?
options: It stays the same each try
It gets smaller with each try
It gets bigger with each try
check.why: She saved 9, then 5, then 3, then 1 second. Practice helps a lot at first, then less and less. Many skills improve like this, quickly and then slowly. The best way to get past the slow part is to keep practising over many days.

setup.caption: 1. Write 1 to 10 in the boxes with your usual hand.

setup.caption: 2. Now use your other hand. Time each try.

experiments.title: Letters or Words: how much can you hold at once?
experiments.context: In this experiment you try to remember 12 letters heard once. First they come in a jumble, then the same letters come as four short words. You see how much grouping helps.
experiments.question: Can you remember more letters when they make words than when they are jumbled?
experiments.predict: The grown-up will read 12 letters in a jumble, then the same 12 letters as four words. How many will you get right each time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both rounds use the same 12 letters. The grown-up reads one letter each second. You say them back straight after, in order. Only the order of the letters changes. Do two jumble rounds and two word rounds with different letters, so one lucky round does not fool you.
results_table: Letters right, in the right place (out of 12)

materials.item: the letter sets on this card. Set 1 jumble: N U P G S O C E P D N U. Set 1 words: DOG SUN CUP PEN. Set 2 jumble: U T N B C A E T S B T A. Set 2 words: CAT BUS NET BAT.
a notebook and pencil for the grown-up

schedule.what: Two jumble rounds and two word rounds. Compare the scores.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each round.

flow.do: Explain the test and ask for a guess with a reason.
flow.say: I will read 12 letters, one each second. You say them back in the same order. First in a jumble, then the same letters as words. Which will be easier? Why?
flow.kid: Listen to 12 letters. Say them back in order. Jumble first, then words. Which is easier? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Letters or Words, a test of how much your short-term memory can hold.

flow.do: 1. Read set 1 jumble, one letter each second: N, U, P, G, S, O, C, E, P, D, N, U. 2. Your child says them back in order straight away. 3. Count how many are right and in the right place.
flow.say: Ready? Listen to all twelve, then say them back. N. U. P. G. S. O. C. E. P. D. N. U. Your turn.
flow.kid: Listen to all twelve letters. Then say them back in order.
flow.parent: Most children of 8 get about 4 to 6 letters in the right place. Do not repeat the letters.

flow.do: 1. Read the set 1 words letter by letter, one each second, with no pauses. 2. Your child says them back. 3. Count the score.
flow.say: The same letters, in a new order. D. O. G. S. U. N. C. U. P. P. E. N. Your turn.
flow.kid: Same letters, new order. Listen. Say them back.
flow.parent: Many children notice the words partway through and get all 12. If they do not notice, that is fine. Write the score down.

flow.do: Do set 2 the same way: jumble first, then words.
flow.say: One more jumble, then one more set of words. Listen carefully.
flow.kid: One more jumble. Then one more set of words.
flow.parent: Set 2 jumble: U, T, N, B, C, A, E, T, S, B, T, A. Set 2 words: C, A, T, B, U, S, N, E, T, B, A, T.

flow.do: Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think made the second round of each set easier? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Why were the words easier? What did you see?
flow.parent: A strong answer: 'Words are easier. I got 5 jumbled letters but all 12 as words. Twelve letters are too many to hold. Four words are only four things.' This is called chunking: grouping many small things into a few bigger ones.

check.q: Why are 12 letters easier as DOG SUN CUP PEN?
options: The letters are bigger
You hold four words instead of twelve separate letters
The grown-up read them more slowly
check.why: Your short-term memory holds only a few things at a time. Twelve separate letters are too many. As four words, they are only four things, and you already know how to spell each one. This is chunking. The letters were the same size and read at the same speed both times.

activities.title: Yesterday's Breakfast: what does your memory keep?
activities.context: This is a starting activity. You try to remember things from yesterday, last month and long ago, and notice which ones your memory kept.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Answer six memory questions. Sort the answers into easy, hard and impossible.

activities.record: Write each question in one of three columns: easy to remember, hard, impossible.

flow.do: Ask the six questions one at a time. Wait for each answer.
flow.say: I will ask you six things. Just tell me what you remember. What did you eat for breakfast yesterday? What did you eat on the same day last month? What is your best friend's name? How do you tie a shoelace? What happened on your last birthday? What were you wearing exactly one week ago?
flow.kid: Answer six questions from memory. Some are easy. Some are very hard!
flow.parent: Most children answer yesterday's breakfast, a friend's name and the birthday easily. Last month's breakfast and last week's clothes are usually impossible. Tying a shoelace is easy to do but hard to explain in words.
flow.context: This is the first step of Yesterday's Breakfast, a short way into the unit on memory.

flow.do: 1. Sort the answers into easy, hard and impossible. 2. Ask what the easy ones have in common.
flow.say: Let's sort them. Which were easy, which were hard, and which were impossible? Why do you think your brain kept some and let others go?
flow.kid: Sort them: easy, hard, impossible. Why did your brain keep some?

ask.q: Why do you remember your birthday but not an ordinary lunch?
good: Because the birthday was special and I felt happy.
Because we talked about it and saw photos.
Because every lunch is nearly the same.

flow.think: Shoelaces were easy to do but hard to explain. Is that a different kind of memory?

setup.caption: 1. Answer six questions from memory.

setup.caption: 2. Sort the answers into three columns.

activities.title: Your Brain in Your Hands: how big and how heavy?
activities.context: In this activity you find out about how big and how heavy a brain is, using your fists and a water bottle.

materials.item: a one-litre plastic water bottle, full
a small cup of water, about 250 ml, or a second small bottle
a cloth bag

schedule.what: Put your fists together to see a brain's size. Lift a bottle that weighs as much as a grown-up's brain.

activities.record: Draw your two fists together and write: my brain is about this big.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to make two fists and put them together, knuckles touching. 2. Hold them up beside their head.
flow.say: Make two fists and put them together like this. Your brain is about this big. It sits inside your skull, behind your forehead and eyes, and all the way to the back of your head.
flow.kid: Make two fists. Put them together. Your brain is about this big!
flow.parent: Two fists together is a common rough guide. By about age 6, a child's brain is already about 90% of its grown-up size. The head keeps growing a little, but most growth after that is in the links, not the size.
flow.context: This is the first step of Your Brain in Your Hands, about the size and weight of a brain.

flow.do: 1. Put the full one-litre bottle and the small cup of water in the cloth bag. 2. Let your child lift it. 3. Ask how it feels.
flow.say: A grown-up's brain weighs about 1.3 kilograms. This bag is about that heavy. Lift it. Your brain uses about a fifth of the energy from all your food. Why do you think it needs so much?
flow.kid: Lift the bag. A grown-up's brain is this heavy. Why does it need so much food?

check.q: A brain is about 2% of the body's weight. How much of the body's energy does it use?
options: Almost none
About a fifth
All of it
check.why: The brain uses about one fifth of the body's energy, even though it is small. Its billions of neurons are sending signals all day and all night, even while you sleep. That is one reason a brain that wasted most of itself would make no sense.

setup.caption: 1. Two fists together are about the size of a brain.

activities.title: Make a Neuron from Dough
activities.context: In this activity you make two model neurons from dough or clay, and show how a message crosses the gap between them.

materials.item: a lump of atta dough the size of an orange, or play clay
a pinch of rava or rice grains
a steel plate to work on

activities.safety: Wash hands after playing with dough. Do not eat raw dough.

schedule.what: Make two neurons from dough. Show a message crossing the gap with rava grains.

activities.record: Draw your neuron and label the middle, the branches, the tail and the gap.

flow.do: 1. Roll a ball of dough for the middle of the neuron. 2. Add five or six short thin branches on one side. 3. Add one long thin tail on the other side. 4. Make a second neuron the same way.
flow.say: A neuron is a nerve cell. It has a round middle, short branches that receive messages, and one long tail that sends them on. Let's make two.
flow.kid: Make a ball. Add short branches. Add one long tail. Make two!
flow.parent: Real neurons are far too small to see without a microscope. The long tail is called the axon, and the branches are called dendrites. You do not need these words yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make a Neuron, where you build model nerve cells from dough.

flow.do: 1. Lay the tail of the first neuron near a branch of the second, with a tiny gap. 2. Drop a few rava grains into the gap. 3. Explain what they stand for.
flow.say: The two neurons do not quite touch. There is a tiny gap called a synapse. The message runs down the tail as electricity. Then it crosses the gap as chemicals, like these grains. What do you think happens if this gap is used again and again?
flow.kid: Leave a tiny gap. Drop grains in the gap. That is the message crossing!

ask.q: What might happen to a synapse that is used many times?

flow.parent: Each real neuron has synapses with thousands of others. When a synapse is used again and again, the message crosses it more easily. That is one way the brain learns.

setup.caption: 1. Make a neuron: a middle, branches and a tail.

setup.art: Two dough neurons with a tiny gap between a tail and a branch, and a few rava grains in the gap.
setup.caption: 2. Leave a gap. The grains are the message crossing it.

activities.title: The Path in the Flour: a model of practice
activities.context: In this activity you make a model of how practice strengthens a path. You draw one line in flour once, and another line ten times.

materials.item: a steel plate with a thin layer of rice flour, kolam powder or atta, about as thick as a coin
a steel spoon

activities.safety: No safety risks. Do it on a sheet of newspaper to catch spills.

schedule.what: Draw one line once and another line ten times. Tap the plate and see which line lasts.

activities.record: Draw the plate after tapping. Write which line stayed and why.

flow.do: 1. Spread the flour evenly. 2. With one finger, draw line A from one side of the plate to the other, once. 3. Draw line B the same way, then trace exactly over it nine more times.
flow.say: Draw line A once. Now draw line B, and go over the same line again and again, ten times in all. Count with me.
flow.kid: Draw line A once. Draw line B ten times, on the same line.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Path in the Flour, a model of how practice changes a path.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess. 2. Tap the edge of the plate gently with the spoon, five times. 3. Look at both lines.
flow.say: If I tap the plate, the flour will shift. Which line do you think will fade first? Why?
flow.kid: Guess which line will fade. Tap the plate five times. Look!
flow.parent: The flour slides into the shallow line A first, so it blurs or fades. The deep line B stays clear for longer. If both stay, tap a little harder.

flow.do: Talk about what the model shows, and what it does not.
flow.say: Line B was used ten times, so it was deeper and lasted longer. In your brain, a path of neurons that is used again and again gets stronger too. But this is only a model. A brain has no flour, and its paths are links between neurons.
flow.kid: Line B was used more. It lasted longer. Brain paths are like that too.

check.q: In the model, what does tracing line B ten times stand for?
options: Practising something many times
Forgetting something
Sleeping
check.why: Tracing the same line again and again stands for practice. Each time you practise, the links between the neurons you use get stronger, like the line getting deeper. The model is not a picture of a real brain. It only shows that using a path again and again makes it last.

setup.caption: 1. Draw line A once, and line B ten times.

setup.caption: 2. Tap the plate. Which line lasts?

activities.title: A Memory Walk Through Your Home
activities.context: In this activity you learn a trick used by memory champions. You put ten things to remember in ten places along a walk through your home.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Choose ten places in your home. Put ten things there in your mind. Walk through them and recall all ten.

activities.record: Draw a map of your memory walk with the ten places numbered.

flow.do: 1. Walk through the flat with your child. 2. Choose ten places in order. For example: front door, shoe rack, sofa, TV, dining table, sink, fridge, bucket, bed, window. 3. Walk them twice.
flow.say: This trick is more than two thousand years old. First we choose ten places in our home, in order. Let's walk them together, twice.
flow.kid: Choose ten places in your home. Walk past them in order.
flow.parent: An old story, told by the Roman writer Cicero, says the poet Simonides of Ceos invented this trick. It is a legend, but the trick is real. Memory champions still use it, and it is called the method of loci, which means 'the method of places'.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Memory Walk, a way to remember a list by placing it around your home.

flow.do: 1. Read this list slowly: elephant, pressure cooker, rainbow, football, coconut, aeroplane, drum, lotus, ice cream, toothbrush. 2. For each one, your child pictures it doing something odd in the next place on the walk.
flow.say: I will read ten things. Put each one in the next place on our walk, and picture it doing something silly. An elephant is stuck in our front door. A pressure cooker is whistling on the shoe rack.
flow.kid: Put each thing in the next place. Make the picture silly!
flow.parent: The odder and more detailed the picture, the better it works. Let your child make up their own pictures after the first two.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to close their eyes and walk through the places in their mind. 2. Ask what they see in each place. 3. Tick the list.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Walk through our home in your mind. What is at the front door? What is on the shoe rack? Keep going.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Walk through your home. What is in each place?
flow.parent: Many children get eight to ten. Ask again tomorrow without warning. Places you know well give each picture something solid to hold on to.

check.q: Why does the memory walk help?
options: Each thing is joined to a place you already know well
Walking makes your legs remember
It works only for clever people
check.why: You know your home very well, so its places are strong memories already. Joining each new thing to a place gives it something to hold on to. The silly picture adds more links. Anyone can use it. Memory champions are not born different, they practise tricks like this.

setup.caption: 1. Choose ten places in order.

setup.art: A cartoon elephant stuck in a front door, and a whistling pressure cooker on a shoe rack.

activities.title: Colour and Number Pairs: Mary Calkins' test
activities.context: In this activity you try a memory test invented by Mary Whiton Calkins in the 1890s. You learn colours paired with numbers, and find out which pairs you remember best.

materials.item: 8 crayons, colour pencils or squares of coloured paper, all different colours
a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Learn eight colour and number pairs. Some pairs are shown three times. Test which pairs you remember.

activities.record: Make a table: colour, number, times shown, remembered or not.

flow.do: Tell your child about Mary Calkins, then explain the test.
flow.say: Mary Calkins was an American scientist. In the 1890s she invented this test. Harvard University refused to give her a degree because she was a woman. I will show you a colour and say a number. Later I show the colour, and you say the number.
flow.kid: I show a colour and say a number. Later, you say the number!
flow.parent: Calkins did all the work for a doctorate at Harvard in 1895, and her examiners praised it highly, but Harvard refused to give women degrees. She later led two of America's biggest groups of psychologists and philosophers. Her paired test is still used in memory research.
flow.context: This is the first step of Colour and Number Pairs, a memory test from the 1890s.

flow.do: 1. Show each crayon for about 3 seconds while saying a two-digit number. 2. Show two of the colours three times each, spread through the list, always with the same number. 3. Show the others once. 4. Write down every pair.
flow.say: Red, 47. Blue, 82. Green, 15. Yellow, 63. Red, 47. Brown, 29. Pink, 91. Blue, 82. Orange, 36. Black, 58. Red, 47. Blue, 82.
flow.kid: Watch each colour. Listen to its number.
flow.parent: In this list red and blue are shown three times. Change the colours to the crayons you have, but keep two of them shown three times.

flow.do: 1. Count back from 20 together. 2. Show each colour once, in a new order, and ask for its number. 3. Tick the right ones.
flow.say: Count back from 20 with me. Now, what number went with this colour? And this one?
flow.kid: Count back from 20. Then say the number for each colour.
flow.parent: Most children get the colours shown three times right much more often than the others. Calkins found that how often a pair was seen mattered more than anything else she tested.

check.q: Which pairs did most children remember best in this test?
options: The ones shown three times
The ones shown last
The ones with small numbers
check.why: Seeing a pair again and again strengthens the link between the colour and the number. Calkins found that how often a pair came up mattered most. The last pairs can be remembered well too, because they are freshest, so check your own results to see.

setup.caption: 1. See a colour and hear its number.

setup.caption: 2. See the colour again. Say its number.

projects.title: My 7-Day Practice Diary
projects.context: In this project you choose one new skill and practise it for ten minutes a day for seven days. You measure it every day to see how practice changes you.

materials.item: a notebook for the diary
a phone stopwatch
whatever your skill needs: rice flour for a kolam, a skipping rope, a ball, a book of Thirukkural or rhymes

projects.safety: Choose a safe skill. Skipping and ball skills need clear space away from furniture, glass and stairs.

schedule.what: Choose a skill. Decide what number you will measure. Do it once and write down the number. Then practise for ten minutes.
Measure first, then practise for ten minutes.
Measure, then draw a graph of all seven days and write what changed.

projects.record: Each day, write the date, your number, and one sentence about how it felt. On day 7, draw a line graph.

flow.do: 1. Help your child choose one skill they cannot yet do well. 2. Choose a number to measure each day. 3. Measure it once. 4. Practise for ten minutes.
flow.say: Choose something you cannot do well yet. It could be a five-dot kolam, catching a ball 20 times, skipping, or saying a Thirukkural couplet. How will we measure it each day?
flow.kid: Choose a new skill. How will you measure it? Try it once.
flow.parent: Good numbers to measure: catches in a row without dropping, skips in a row, seconds to draw a kolam, or words of a couplet said without help. Measure before practising each day, so the number shows what stayed overnight.
flow.context: This is the first day of a 7-day project. You practise one new skill each day and measure how it changes.

flow.do: On days 2 to 6, measure first, then practise for ten minutes. Write the number in the diary.
flow.say: Measure first, before practising. Write down your number. Now practise for ten minutes.
flow.kid: Measure first. Write the number. Then practise ten minutes.
flow.wait: Do this every day, from day 2 to day 6.
flow.parent: Some days the number will go down. That is normal. Practice works over many days, not in a straight line.

flow.do: On day 7, measure one last time, draw a line graph, and talk about it.
flow.say: Let's draw a graph of all seven days. What changed? Your arms and legs are the same as last week. So what changed?
flow.kid: Draw your seven numbers as a line. What changed? Where?

check.q: After seven days, Sneha could skip 40 times instead of 8. What changed most?
options: Her legs grew much longer
The links in her brain for skipping got stronger
The rope got lighter
check.why: In one week, her legs and the rope stayed the same. Each day of practice strengthened the links between the neurons that time her jumps and swing the rope. Her muscles may have got a little stronger too, but the big change was in her brain.

setup.caption: 1. Choose a skill and a number to measure.

setup.art: A girl skipping with a rope in a flat's hall, with furniture pushed back.
setup.caption: 2. Measure, then practise ten minutes every day.

challenges.title: Help Thatha Remember
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a way to help someone remember to do something every day.
challenges.problem: Thatha, a grandfather, keeps forgetting whether he has taken his evening tablet. Design a reminder that helps him know, every evening, whether he has already done it.
constraints: Use only paper, cardboard, pens, clips and things from home.
It must show clearly whether today's tablet is done.
It must be easy to use with one hand.
You never touch the real tablets. A grown-up handles medicines.
materials: an empty matchbox or small box
general: A pill box with one space for each day of the week, so an empty space shows the tablet is taken.
A chart on the wall with a tick for each day.
An alarm on a phone at the same time every evening.
creative: A clothes peg that moves along a strip of the seven days each time the tablet is taken.
A card hung on the door handle, with 'done' on one side and 'not yet' on the other.
Linking the tablet to something Thatha already does every evening, like the 7 o'clock news, so the habit carries it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own reminder. Draw it, make a model, and test it on a grown-up for three days with a pretend task.

flow.do: Read the problem together and talk about why people forget daily tasks.
flow.say: Why is it hard to remember whether you did something today? Every evening is nearly the same, so the memories mix together.
flow.kid: Why is it hard to remember? Every evening looks the same!
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a reminder to help a grandfather remember his evening tablet.

flow.do: 1. Draw two ideas. 2. Choose one and build a model from cardboard and pegs.
flow.say: Draw two ideas. Then choose one and build it. Your reminder must show at a glance whether today is done.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas. Build one. Can you tell at a glance?
flow.parent: A grown-up helps with scissors. Your child should test the model with a pretend task, such as drinking a glass of water at 7 o'clock, never with real medicines.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas, then improve the design.
flow.say: Here are some ideas other people use. Which is most like yours? Can you make yours better?
flow.kid: Look at other ideas. Can you make yours better?

check.q: Why does linking the tablet to the 7 o'clock news help Thatha?
options: The news reminds him of the task he does at the same time every day
The news is loud
It makes the tablet work better
check.why: When a new task is joined to something you already do every day, the old habit brings the new task back to mind. Doing it at the same time and place again and again turns it into a habit too.

setup.art: A drawing of an elderly man in a veshti sitting in an armchair, looking puzzled at a small box.
setup.caption: 1. The problem: did Thatha take his tablet today?

setup.art: A cardboard strip with seven days written on it and a clothes peg clipped on one day.
setup.caption: 2. Build a reminder that shows if today is done.

challenges.title: Twenty Things Tomorrow
challenges.context: This is a memory challenge. You must remember a list of 20 things until tomorrow, without writing it down, using any tricks you like.
challenges.problem: Amma is going to the market tomorrow and has lost her pen. Remember her list of 20 things until tomorrow evening, with no writing.
constraints: No writing or drawing the list.
You hear the list once, slowly, and you get ten minutes to use your tricks.
You must say the list tomorrow, at least 24 hours later.
materials: The list, read by a grown-up: rice, dal, salt, sugar, milk, curd, eggs, butter, tomatoes, onions, potatoes, carrots, bananas, apples, mangoes, grapes, soap, toothpaste, a bucket, a broom.
general: Group the list: things for the kitchen shelf, the fridge, the vegetable shop, the fruit shop and for cleaning.
Make a story that joins all twenty.
Put each thing in a place on a memory walk through your home.
creative: Use the first letters to make a silly sentence.
Sing the list to a song you already know.
Act out each thing with your hands as you say it.
challenges.your_turn: Make up your own memory trick for a list of 20 things. Teach it to someone in your family and test them tomorrow.

flow.do: Read the list once, slowly, while your child listens.
flow.say: Here is Amma's list of twenty things. Listen once. Then you have ten minutes to use any trick you like.
flow.kid: Listen to twenty things. Then use your best tricks!
flow.context: This is a memory challenge. You remember a list of 20 things until tomorrow without writing anything.

flow.do: Give your child ten minutes to use any tricks. They may ask for the list to be read once more.
flow.say: Which tricks will you use? You could group them, make a story, or walk them round our home.
flow.kid: Group them? A story? A memory walk? Choose your tricks.
flow.parent: Grouping usually helps most with this list. It splits into five groups of four: kitchen shelf, fridge, vegetables, fruit and cleaning. Let your child choose.

flow.do: The next evening, ask your child to say the whole list. Count how many they remember.
flow.say: It is market time. Can you tell me all twenty things on Amma's list?
flow.kid: Say Amma's whole list. How many can you remember?

check.q: Pooja grouped the list into kitchen shelf, fridge, vegetables, fruit and cleaning. Why does this help?
options: She remembers five groups, and each group brings back its four things
Groups make the list shorter
Shops are easy to spell
check.why: Five groups are easy to hold. When she remembers 'fridge', it brings back milk, curd, eggs and butter. The list is still twenty things long, but now it has a shape that links them.
