quiz.p: Which of these is a job of your brain?
quiz.why: Remembering is a brain job. The heart pumps blood, and the stomach and gut break down food, though the brain helps control them.

quiz.p: How do neurons pass messages to each other?
opts: A message crosses a tiny gap called a synapse
They send light to each other
quiz.why: A message runs along a neuron as an electrical signal, then crosses the synapse as a chemical. Neurons do not swap places or send light.

quiz.p: Knowing how to swim is which kind of memory?
quiz.why: Swimming is a skill memory: your body knows how to do it without thinking of the steps. It lasts a long time, so it is not short-term.

quiz.p: Why does a skill get easier with practice?
opts: The links between the neurons you use get stronger
Your brain gets heavier every day
quiz.why: Each time you practise, the links between the neurons you use get stronger, so the signal passes more easily. Your brain does not get noticeably heavier.

quiz.p: Kalyani learned list A by repeating it and list B by making a story. To make the test fair, what must be the same?
opts: The number and kind of words, and the time for each word
quiz.why: Both lists need the same number of similar words and the same time, so only the way of learning changes. The words must be different, or the second list would be easier.

quiz.p: In the Story Trick, most children remember far more of the story list the next day. What does this show?
opts: What you do with words while you learn them changes how well you remember them
Memory is better in the morning
quiz.why: Both lists had similar words, and only the way of learning changed. So the story helped. Testing at the same time of day rules out the time.

quiz.p: Which way of remembering a list of 20 things uses grouping?
opts: Putting them into fridge things, vegetables and fruit
quiz.why: Grouping puts many things into a few groups. Each group then brings back the things in it.

quiz.p: Which is the best way to remember a times table for a long time?
opts: Read it ten times on one day
Say it from memory on many different days
quiz.why: Recalling it on many days makes the memory stronger each time. Reading many times on one day fades quickly.

quiz.p: Is it true that we use only 10% of our brain?
opts: No, every part of the brain is used
quiz.why: Brain scans show every part of the brain working over a day. The 10% idea is a myth.

quiz.p: What did the study of trainee taxi drivers in London show?
opts: Grown-up brains can change when they learn
quiz.why: Trainees who learned the city's streets and passed grew a bigger back part of the hippocampus. Their brains had matched other people's before. So grown-up brains change with learning.

quiz.p: A touch-me-not plant was dropped gently many times and stopped folding their leaves. What had happened?
opts: The plant had learned that the drop was harmless
quiz.why: The plants learned the drop was harmless and kept that memory for weeks. They still folded when shaken in a new way, so they were not dead or worn out.

quiz.p: Which of these beings can learn and remember?
quiz.why: People, bees, dogs and even touch-me-not plants learn from what happened before. Each does it in their own way.

items.p: What are neurons?
opts: Drops of blood in the brain
items.why: Neurons are nerve cells. They carry messages as tiny electrical signals, and your brain has about 86 billion of them. The skull is bone, and blood flows through the brain, but neither carries the messages.
items.art: One neuron with branches and a long tail.

items.p: Your brain keeps working while you sleep.
items.why: True. While you sleep, your brain keeps your heart beating and your lungs breathing. It also helps the day's new memories settle.

items.p: The tiny gap where one neuron passes its message to the next is called a ____.
items.why: A synapse is the tiny gap between two neurons. The message crosses it as a chemical.

items.p: Match each memory to its kind.
pairs: a memory of something that happened
Knowing that Chennai is in Tamil Nadu
Holding an OTP in your head while you type it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A strong answer sees that memories differ in what they keep: a time and a place, a fact, a way of moving, or a few things held for a few seconds.

items.p: Sort these. Does your brain do it while you notice, or without you noticing?
items: choosing a sweet at a shop
making you shiver in the cold
items.a: see items
items.why: Your brain does many jobs you never notice, like your heartbeat and breathing in sleep. Thinking and remembering are the jobs you notice.

items.p: In the Story Trick, you count backwards from 20 after hearing each list. Why?
opts: To make the test harder for the story list
To stop you repeating the words in your head, so both lists wait the same way
items.why: Counting backwards keeps your mind busy, so you cannot keep saying the words to yourself. Both lists then wait in the same way, which makes the test fair.

items.p: Most forgetting happens in the first day after you learn something.
items.why: True. Hermann Ebbinghaus found this in 1885, and many later studies agree. After the first day, forgetting slows down. That is why recalling something the next day helps so much.

items.p: Leela, a girl in Class 3, must remember her mother's mobile number, 9841023456. Which is the best way?
items.why: Two groups of five are much easier to hold than ten separate digits. This is chunking. Saying it fast does not help you keep it.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, to show how a new memory is made and kept.
items: link it to something you already know
recall it again on another day
hold it in your mind for a few seconds
a: hold it in your mind for a few seconds
link it to something you already know
recall it again on another day
items.why: First you must notice something. Then short-term memory holds it. Linking it to what you know helps your brain keep it, and recalling it on later days makes it last.

items.p: Kavya, a girl of eight, practised a kolam with her right hand every morning for a month. Then she tried it with her left hand, and it went wrong. Why?
items.a: Her left hand has the same kind of muscles, but it had not practised. The practice had made strong links in her brain for drawing with her right hand, not her left.
items.why: A strong answer says that the skill was built by practice, in the links of the brain for that hand, and that the left hand had not been given that practice.

items.p: Draw two neurons with a gap between them. Draw an arrow to show which way the message goes.
items.a: Two neurons, each with a round middle, branches and a tail. The tail of the first is close to a branch of the second, with a small gap. The arrow goes along the first neuron's tail, across the gap, into the second.
items.why: A good drawing shows the gap, the synapse, and the message going from the tail of one neuron to the branches of the next.
items.art: A blank box with a small dotted line in the middle.

items.p: We use only 10% of our brain.
items.why: False. Brain scans show every part of the brain working over a day, and damage to almost any part causes problems. The 10% idea is an old myth.

items.p: Grouping many small things into a few bigger pieces, so they are easier to remember, is called ____.
items.why: Chunking turns many small things into a few bigger ones, like twelve letters into four words.

items.p: Write about one thing you can now do without thinking, which was hard when you started. How did it become easy?
items.a: For example: 'I can ride my cycle without thinking. At first I fell a lot. I practised every evening, and it got easier each week.'
items.why: A strong answer names a real skill and says that doing it again and again, over many days, made it easy.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Riding a cycle, swimming, tying shoelaces, knowing the capital of Kerala.
items.a: knowing the capital of Kerala
items.why: The capital of Kerala is Thiruvananthapuram. Knowing it is a fact. The other three are skill memories: things your body knows how to do.

items.p: In the Other Hand experiment, Shalini wrote 1 to 10 with her other hand ten times over three days. Which result shows that practice worked?
opts: Her first try took 55 seconds and her tenth took 33
items.why: Her time fell from 55 to 33 seconds with practice. If every try took the same time, practice would not have changed anything. Her usual hand's time is a comparison, not a result of practice.

items.p: Meenakshi and Farhan, two children in Class 4, disagree about memory.

views.says: Some people are just born with a better memory. My cousin remembers everything without trying.
Anyone can have a good memory. It depends on practice and on the tricks you use.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from what you tested. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence, for example the Story Trick, where the same child remembered far more with a story. It also says what the other side has right: people do differ a little, and some of that may come from birth.
items.why: Both have a point. People differ somewhat in memory, partly from birth. But the tricks and practice a person uses make a much bigger difference, and memory champions say they trained, not that they were born that way.

items.p: The curved part deep inside the brain, shaped like a seahorse, that helps store new memories of events and places, is called the ____.
items.why: The hippocampus helps store new memories of events and places. Its name is Greek for 'seahorse'.

items.p: A grown-up's brain cannot change any more.
items.why: False. Grown-up brains keep changing as they learn. London taxi drivers grew a bigger part of the hippocampus while they learned thousands of streets.

items.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 3, wants to remember a poem for a show in one month. Which plan will help her most?
opts: Read it ten times on Monday, then rest
Say it from memory for a few minutes on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, and check it each time
Read it once the night before the show
items.why: Saying it from memory on different days makes the memory stronger each time. Reading it many times on one day helps on that day, but most of it fades quickly. One reading the night before is too little.

items.p: Your friend Sanjana did the Story Trick. Straight away, she remembered 6 words from each list. The next day she remembered 2 repeated words and 7 story words. Why did the difference show only the next day?
items.a: Straight away, both lists were still fresh in short-term memory. By the next day the repeated words had mostly faded, because each one stood alone. The story words were linked to each other and to pictures, so they lasted.
items.why: A strong answer explains that short-term memory hides the difference at first, and that links between the story words help them last overnight.

items.p: Sort these. Do they help you remember for a long time, or not much?
items: making a story from the list
reading the same page again and again
staying up all night before a test
learning a little on many days
items.a: see items
items.why: Stories, sleep, testing yourself and spreading learning over days all strengthen memories. Reading again and again feels good but adds few new links. Staying up all night takes away the sleep that helps memories settle.

items.p: Match each memory trick to the reason it works.
pairs: each word leads to the next
each thing is joined to a place you know well
you hold a few groups instead of many small things
bringing a memory back makes it stronger
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every trick works by giving the new thing more links, or by giving your short-term memory fewer things to hold.

items.p: A honeybee visits blue flowers that have lots of nectar and yellow flowers that have none. The next day, which flowers will she most likely visit first?
opts: Any colour, because bees do not learn
items.why: Honeybees learn which colours give nectar and remember it for days. She has learned that blue flowers are worth visiting. Bees do learn, so the last option is wrong.

items.p: Draw the shape of the line graph you would expect for ten tries of writing with your other hand. Label the bottom 'try' and the side 'seconds'. Write one sentence about the shape.
items.a: A line that starts high, falls quickly over the first few tries, then falls more slowly. 'I got faster quickly at first, then more slowly.'
items.why: A strong answer shows the line going down, and steeper at the start than at the end.

items.p: In an experiment, touch-me-not plants learned that being dropped gently was harmless, and remembered it for weeks.
items.why: True. In 2014 Monica Gagliano and her team dropped touch-me-not plants a short way again and again. The plants stopped folding their leaves, and still remembered almost a month later.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how practice makes a skill easy.
items: the skill becomes faster and smoother
the first try is slow and wobbly
you can do it without thinking
the links you use get a little stronger each time
a: the first try is slow and wobbly
the links you use get a little stronger each time
the skill becomes faster and smoother
you can do it without thinking
items.why: Practice strengthens the links between neurons step by step. As they strengthen, the skill gets faster, until it needs no thought.

items.p: Why is it easier to remember the words of a song than the same words written as a plain list?
items.a: The tune and the rhythm join the words together, and each line leads to the next. In a plain list, each word stands alone.
items.why: A strong answer says the tune adds links between the words, the same way a story does.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Hippocampus, neuron, synapse, kidney.
items.a: kidney
items.why: The kidney cleans the blood. The hippocampus, neurons and synapses are all parts of the brain's way of thinking and remembering.

items.p: Rani, a girl of eight, hears a list of digits once and says them back. About how many can most children of her age hold?
items.why: Most children of 8 can hold about 5 digits heard once, and most grown-ups about 7. That is why longer numbers are easier in groups.

items.p: Two scientists disagree about the touch-me-not plants that stopped folding after being dropped many times.

views.says: The plants learned that the drop was harmless and remembered it for weeks. That is memory, without any brain.
Memory is what neurons do. The plants only got tired of folding, or made a simple automatic change.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what the experiment found. Then answer back from the other side.
items.a: A strong answer uses the evidence: the plants still folded when shaken in a new way, so they were not just tired, and they kept the change for almost a month. The other side could say that memory in people needs neurons and is far richer.
items.why: In the experiment, the plants still folded when shaken in a new way, so tiredness does not explain it. Scientists still argue about whether to call this learning. A strong answer weighs both.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether sleep helps you remember. What would you do, and what would you keep the same?
items.a: Learn one list of ten words in the morning and test it in the evening, with no sleep in between. Learn a second, similar list in the evening and test it the next morning, after sleep. Keep the same number and kind of words, the same time to learn, and the same 12 hours of waiting.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing, sleep or no sleep, and keeps the words, the learning time and the waiting time the same.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 4, says, 'I am a picture learner. I can only learn from pictures.' How could you test whether this is true?
items.a: Give him ten words to learn by hearing them, and ten different but similar words to learn from pictures. Test both the next day. Then do the same with other children. If almost everyone does better with pictures, the pictures help everyone, not only 'picture learners'.
items.why: When scientists tested this, people did not learn more in their own favourite style. Pictures help most people. A strong answer compares both ways for Arjun and for others.

items.p: Scientists found that London taxi drivers had a bigger back part of the hippocampus. Then they scanned trainee drivers before they started learning the streets. Why?
opts: To check whether people with a big hippocampus simply chose to become drivers
Because scans are cheaper for trainees
items.why: If drivers were born with a bigger hippocampus, learning would not explain it. The trainees' brains matched other people's at the start. Only those who learned the streets and passed showed the growth. So the learning caused the change.

items.p: Each time you recall a memory, your brain builds it again, so a memory can change over time.
items.why: True. Memories are rebuilt each time we recall them. That is why two people can remember the same day differently, and why a memory is not an exact recording.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 5, says, 'I read my notes ten times, so I will remember them for the test.' What is the best advice for her?
opts: Close the notes and test herself, on a few different days
items.why: Reading again and again feels easy, but it adds few links. Trying to bring the notes back without looking, on different days, makes the memory much stronger. Copying neatly helps a little, but less.

items.p: When the same synapse is used again and again, the message crosses it more ____.
items.why: A synapse that is used often gets stronger, so the message passes more easily. This is how practice changes the brain.

items.p: Label the drawing of a neuron: the middle, the branches, the long tail, and the gap to the next neuron.
items.why: The branches receive messages, the middle holds the cell's centre, the tail sends the message on, and the gap is where it crosses to the next neuron.
items.art: A neuron with four blank label lines pointing to its middle, branches, tail and a gap at the end of the tail.

items.p: Imagine you could never forget anything at all. Give one good thing and one bad thing about it.
items.a: Good: I would never lose a name or a fact. Bad: I would remember every boring lunch and every bad moment, and it might be hard to find the important things among them.
items.why: A strong answer sees that forgetting is useful. It clears away what does not matter, so the important memories stand out.

items.p: Paati, a grandmother in Madurai, has many memories. Sort them by kind.
items: how to draw a sikku kolam
that Madurai is on the Vaigai river
the first time she saw the sea
that a week has seven days
items.a: see items
items.why: Memories of events have a time and a place. Facts are things known without remembering when you learned them. Skills are done by the body without thinking of the steps.

items.p: In Letters or Words, Arjun got all 12 letters right as words, but only 5 as a jumble. His sister Suha says the words were read more slowly. How could they check?
opts: Use a stopwatch to read both rounds at one letter each second
Do only the word round again
items.why: If both rounds are read at the same speed, speed cannot explain the difference. Only the order of the letters should change. Asking Arjun tells us what he felt, not what caused it.

items.p: Practising for 10 minutes on each of 6 days usually helps more than practising for one hour on one day.
items.why: True. The total time is the same, an hour. But practice spread over days gives the brain time and sleep to strengthen the links, and each new day brings the memory back again.

items.p: A Carnatic music teacher in Chennai makes new students sing the same simple exercises every day for months before they learn songs. Why?
opts: So the patterns become strong enough to sing without thinking
Because the teacher has forgotten the songs
items.why: Daily practice strengthens the links for the notes and patterns, until they come without effort. Then the student's attention is free for the song itself.

items.p: Your brain changes every time you learn something. Are you the same person you were last year? Give a reason.
items.a: Any answer with a reason. For example: 'Partly. My brain has new links from everything I learned, so I am a bit different. But I still have my old memories and my name, so I am still me.'
items.why: A strong answer uses the science, that learning changes the brain, and thinks about what stays the same as well as what changes.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Making a story, grouping, a memory walk, reading the same page ten times.
items.a: reading the same page ten times
items.why: Making a story, grouping and a memory walk all give new things links to each other or to things you know. Reading the same page again adds very few new links.

applications: Teachers space out revision over weeks and give short quizzes, because recalling on different days makes memories last.
Phone numbers, bank account numbers and number plates are written in groups, so people can hold them more easily.
Musicians, dancers and sportspeople practise the same small moves every day until they need no thought.
Doctors and therapists help people who have had a stroke to practise movements, so the brain can build new links around the damage.
Pill boxes with one space for each day help people remember whether they have taken their medicine.
Memory champions use memory walks and stories to remember hundreds of numbers or words.
Many families in India have passed down songs, stories and recipes by memory, from grandparents to grandchildren, for generations.
Scientists who study memory are looking for ways to help people with Alzheimer's disease, an illness that slowly takes away memories.

open_questions.q: How do signals between neurons become the experience of remembering?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can see which neurons fire when we remember, but nobody knows how that becomes the feeling of seeing your grandmother's face in your mind.

open_questions.q: Why do we sleep, and exactly what does sleep do to memories?
open_questions.why_open: Sleep clearly helps memories settle, and memory areas replay the day in sleep. But scientists still argue about exactly how this works and why it needs sleep.

open_questions.q: How do plants and single-celled beings keep memories without neurons?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments show they learn and remember, but scientists are only beginning to find out what inside them holds the memory.

open_questions.q: Why do we forget almost everything from before the age of three?
open_questions.why_open: Young children learn huge amounts, but most grown-ups remember nothing from their first years. There are several ideas, and none is proven.

maths.problem: In the Story Trick, Meena remembered 3 words from her repeated list and 8 words from her story list the next day. Each list had 10 words. How many more story words did she remember? What fraction of each list did she remember?
maths.answer: 5 more story words. She remembered 3 tenths of the repeated list and 8 tenths of the story list.
maths.explain: 8 - 3 = 5, so 5 more. Each list had 10 words. 3 out of 10 is three tenths. 8 out of 10 is eight tenths.
maths.context: This is about the Story Trick, where you learn one list by repeating it and one by making a story.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you compare her results with a friend who used lists of a different length.

chart.title: Meena's words remembered the next day

maths.problem: Ravi wrote 1 to 10 with his other hand. His times were 50, 44, 40, 38 and 37 seconds. How many seconds did he save on each new try? Guess his time on the sixth try, and say why.
maths.answer: He saved 6, 4, 2 and 1 seconds. A good guess for the sixth try is about 36 or 37 seconds.
maths.explain: 50 - 44 = 6. 44 - 40 = 4. 40 - 38 = 2. 38 - 37 = 1. The savings get smaller each time, so the next one is probably about 1 second or less.
maths.context: This is about the Other Hand experiment, where you time yourself writing with the hand you do not usually use.
maths.why_maths: Working out the gaps between the numbers shows the pattern of practice, so you can predict the next try.

maths.problem: A grown-up's brain weighs about 1300 grams. A full one-litre bottle of water weighs about 1000 grams. How much more water must you add to match the brain? About how many 100-gram packets of biscuits weigh the same as a brain?
maths.answer: About 300 grams more water. About 13 packets.
maths.explain: 1300 - 1000 = 300 grams. 1300 grams is 13 lots of 100 grams, so 13 packets.
maths.context: This is about Your Brain in Your Hands, where you lift a bag as heavy as a grown-up's brain.
maths.why_maths: Comparing grams with things you can lift makes the weight of a brain something you can feel.

maths.problem: The number plate KA 05 MN 4821 has 10 letters and digits. Shreya says it as KA 05, MN, 48, 21. How many groups is that? If she can hold 5 things in her short-term memory, can she hold the plate as separate letters and digits? As groups?
maths.answer: 4 groups. As 10 separate letters and digits, no. As 4 groups, yes.
maths.explain: KA 05 is one group, MN is one, 48 is one and 21 is one, so 4 groups. 10 things are more than 5, but 4 groups are fewer than 5.
maths.context: This is about Number Plate Flash, where you look at a plate for five seconds and write it from memory.
maths.why_maths: Counting the groups shows why chunking lets a small memory hold a long number.

maths.problem: Divya practised catching a ball for 7 days. Her catches in a row were 4, 7, 9, 8, 12, 14, 15. On which day did her number go down? What was her biggest jump from one day to the next? Why might a number go down for one day?
maths.answer: It went down on day 4, from 9 to 8. The biggest jump was from day 4 to day 5, 4 more catches. A number can dip on a day when you are tired, distracted or unlucky.
maths.explain: The jumps are 3, 2, then down 1, then 4, 2 and 1. One bad day does not mean practice stopped working. The whole line still goes up.
maths.context: This is about the 7-Day Practice Diary, where you practise one skill every day and measure it.
maths.why_maths: Seeing all seven numbers together shows the real pattern, so one bad day does not fool you.

roots.context: We have tested how stories, groups and practice help us remember. Now we ask what memory tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You heard two lists of ten home words, with the same time for each word. The next day, you remembered far more of the list you made into a story. The only change was what your mind did with the words. So how well you remember depends on what you do while you learn.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about a 'good memory' or a 'bad memory' as if it were a box we are born with, big or small. The Story Trick shows that remembering is something you do, and the same child can do it well or badly.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Story Trick, the same child, with the same kind of words and the same time, remembered far more of the story list the next day. Gordon Bower and Michal Clark found the same with grown-ups in 1969.

three.who_am_i: You are partly made by what you practise. Every skill and memory you build changes your brain a little.
three.what_is_life: Living beings learn from what happened to them before, from bees and dogs to touch-me-not plants.
three.what_is_this_world: The places and people you meet leave lasting changes in you. A taxi driver's brain carries the shape of a city's streets.

roots.thread: Every human brain starts from the same plan, with the same kinds of neurons. Then each life uses some links more than others. The links that are used grow stronger, and each brain takes the shape of the life it has lived. So from one shared plan come billions of different minds, each shaped by what they did and met.

teachings.teaching: Memory, smriti, is not letting go of something you have experienced.
teachings.link: In the Story Trick, the story words were the ones your mind did not let go. Patanjali describes memory as holding on, which is what strong links between neurons do.

teachings.teaching: Practice becomes firm when it is done for a long time, without breaks, and with care.
teachings.link: This is what the Other Hand experiment and the 7-Day Practice Diary showed: short practice on many days, done with attention, makes a skill firm.

teachings.teaching: We become builders by building, and lyre players by playing the lyre, a small kind of harp. In the same way, we become fair by doing fair things.
teachings.link: Aristotle saw that what we do again and again shapes what we become. Brain science now shows one way it happens: practice changes the links in the brain.

science.text: Synapses that are used again and again grow stronger, and this is one way the brain stores memories and skills.
How signals between neurons become the experience of remembering is not known.
Plants and single-celled beings learn and remember without neurons. Scientists are still working out how, and some argue about whether to call it learning.

other_view.view: A memory is a pattern of strengthened links between neurons, and nothing more. There is no awareness that holds on to experiences. The brain is all there is to memory, and talk of a mind beyond it adds nothing.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a flat, with the materials listed. The Story Trick needs only a grown-up's voice, a notebook and a phone stopwatch. The repeat list always comes first, so the story habit does not leak into it, and counting back from 20 stops repeating during the wait. Straight away the two lists are often close, so the steps tell the parent the big difference usually shows the next day, and say that close numbers are a real result too. The two word lists use only everyday objects. In Letters or Words, the jumbles were checked to use exactly the same letters as their words, without hidden short words. The Other Hand needs a box grid that can be drawn in pencil. The flour path is a model, and the step says so. Calkins' test keeps two colours shown three times. Medicines are never handled by the child in Help Thatha Remember. The spine is Yesterday's Breakfast, the Story Trick with its 5-minute next-day check, the explanation cards, the flour path, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes over two sessions.

how_we_found_out.story: For much of the 1900s, many scientists thought a grown-up's brain was fixed. Children's brains grow and change, they said, but after that a brain only wears out. In the late 1990s, Eleanor Maguire, a brain scientist in London, studied London's taxi drivers. To get a licence, they must learn about 25,000 streets and the way between any two places. This test is called the Knowledge, and it takes most people three to four years. Maguire and her team scanned the brains of 16 taxi drivers, all men. In 2000 they reported that the back part of the hippocampus, which helps us find our way, was bigger in the drivers than in other men. The longer a man had driven a taxi, the bigger it was. But perhaps people born with a big hippocampus chose to drive taxis? So Katherine Woollett and Maguire scanned 79 trainees before they began, and again three to four years later. At the start, their brains matched other people's. The 39 who passed the Knowledge had grown in that part. Those who gave up, and people who never trained, had not. Learning had changed grown-up brains.
how_we_found_out.who: Eleanor Maguire and her team, and later Katherine Woollett with Eleanor Maguire, at University College London
how_we_found_out.when: 2000 (the taxi driver scans) and 2011 (the trainees scanned before and after)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought the grown-up brain was fixed and could not change its shape. The trainee drivers started with brains like everyone else's, and those who learned the streets grew a bigger back part of the hippocampus. So learning changes grown-up brains too.
